# Speculative Decoding, Flash Attention, and KV-Cache Traffic on a Single GPU

The central tension in large language model inference on a single GPU is the mismatch between the arithmetic intensity of the forward pass and the memory bandwidth available to feed that arithmetic. During the prefill phase, a long prompt is processed in one large matrix-multiply, and the GPU's tensor cores are kept busy because the operation is compute-bound: every FLOP is paired with a proportional number of bytes read from high-bandwidth memory, and the arithmetic intensity comfortably exceeds the roofline threshold of the hardware. The decode phase, by contrast, is a sequence of single-token steps, each of which must read the entire key-value cache from HBM before it can compute even one new token. The arithmetic intensity of a single decode step is vanishingly small relative to the bytes that must be fetched, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory rather than performing useful floating-point work. Every technique that modern inference stacks employ—flash attention, speculative decoding, paged KV caches, quantized projections—is ultimately a negotiation with this single fact: the KV cache is the dominant traffic source on the GPU, and the decode step is the phase in which that traffic becomes the bottleneck.

The key-value cache is the concrete mechanism by which a transformer avoids recomputing attention over the full context at every decode step. After the prefill pass, every layer stores a key and a value vector for each position in the sequence, and these tensors are laid out in HBM in a format that is typically contiguous per layer and per head. When the model generates the next token, the attention kernel must read every stored key and value vector, project the new query against them, and write the updated cache entry. On a single GPU with, say, 1.5 terabytes per second of HBM bandwidth, a model with thirty-two layers, each holding a KV cache of a few megabytes per token, can easily see the decode step dominated by the cost of streaming that cache through the memory hierarchy. The arithmetic performed per byte read is on the order of a handful of multiply-accumulate operations, far below the ratio at which the tensor cores can sustain peak throughput. The GPU is, in effect, a memory device during decode, and the compute pipeline is starved.

Flash attention reframes the attention computation so that it never materializes the full quadratic attention-score matrix in HBM.
